She joined the brand in 2022. People Editorial Guidelines Published on October 23, 2026 11:37AM EDT 7 Comments Add Us On Bentwood Elementary School in Olathe, Kansas (stock image). Credit : Google Maps NEED TO KNOW Nearly 100 students and staff have been linked to a norovirus outbreak at Bentwood Elementary School in Olathe, Kansas Health officials said no hospitalizations were reported and no new cases were reported as of Oct. 13 Norovirus spreads easily through contaminated food surfaces and close contact, making handwashing especially important, the CDC said A norovirus outbreak has affected nearly 100 people at an elementary school in Kansas. There were 95 cases reported among students and staff linked to an outbreak at the Bentwood Elementary School in Olathe, Kansas, a joint statement from Johnson County Department of Health and Environment (JCDHE) and Olathe Public Schools obtained by PEOPLE read. Two more cases were reported among family members outside the school, according to JCDHE Director Charlie Hunt, per KCTV. Norovirus is a highly contagious virus that causes vomiting and diarrhea, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency said the virus spreads “very easily” through contaminated food or liquids, direct contact with an infected person, or touching contaminated objects and surfaces. Symptoms reported by people impacted by the outbreak included vomiting, diarrhea, nausea and stomach pain, per the joint statement. A micrograph of the norovirus (stock image). BSIP/UIG Via Getty Two of the norovirus cases reported at the elementary school were confirmed through laboratory testing, while the remaining cases were considered “epidemiologically linked,” meaning those affected experienced similar symptoms around the same time and in the same setting, suggesting they were part of the same outbreak. “Bentwood Elementary first experienced student absences involving similar illness symptoms on October 8,” per the statement. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. There were no hospitalizations reported during the outbreak, which reportedly occurred during the beginning of October. As of Oct. 13, there had been no new cases reported. The JCDHE confirmed in a social media post on Wednesday, Oct. 21, that the norovirus outbreak at the school was “over.” “Throughout the outbreak, JCDHE worked closely with school officials to monitor illnesses, provide public health guidance and help prevent further spread,” the school district and health department continued in their joint statement. Related Stories Cruise Passengers Hit with Norovirus as Ship Experiences Second Outbreak in a Month Foodborne Parasitic Outbreak That Causes 'Explosive' Diarrhea Has Spread to 17 States “Although the outbreak is considered over, JCDHE and the Olathe Public Schools will continue to monitor the situation and work together to help protect the health of students, staff and families,” they added. Dr. Dana Hawkinson, an infectious disease physician and medical director of infection prevention and control at the University of Kansas Health System, told KCTV that outbreaks like these can be very common. Subscribe Now “It’s very common to see outbreaks or clusters because this virus, when it is shed, again, through the fecal route, is very easy to contaminate places. So it is very important to wash your hands with soap and water to help decrease the contamination around,” Hawkinson said. “But those viruses are very small. And so you don’t know and understand when you have contact with them, especially if you’re in a household.” According to JCDHE Director Hunt, per KCTV, the number of cases was likely higher because of how contagious norovirus is. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. The CDC said norovirus is the leading cause of foodborne illness in the U.S., and causes 58% of foodborne illnesses acquired in the U.S. It is responsible for nearly 1 million pediatric medical care visits annually and it causes 19 to 21 million illnesses on average each year. content: Norovirus Risk Extends Beyond Oysters, with Leafy Greens Linked to 32% of Foodborne Cases by Kim Bo Mi Updated 2026/10/27 13:06 Norovirus can also be contracted through vegetables. /AI-generated photo Norovirus infections surge from November, when the weather turns cold. Oysters are a ëíì ì ̧ food ingredient that raises the risk of infection, but people can also contract norovirus through vegetables. Norovirus can survive even at minus 20Â°C. It can enter the body through contaminated ingredients, including seafood as well as fruits and vegetables. In particular, vegetables stored in the refrigerator should not be eaten without washing them. An investigation by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, CDC, into foods linked to norovirus outbreaks from 1998 to 2008 found that leafy greens accounted for the highest proportion, at 32%. Vegetables should be washed thoroughly before eating. /AI-generated photo When washing vegetables, soak them in water first and then rinse them thoroughly under running water. The MFDS analyzed the effectiveness of different washing methods in removing norovirus from lettuce and perilla leaves that had been artificially contaminated with the virus. The analysis found that soaking them in water for 2 minutes and then washing them under running water for 30 seconds removed 87.5% and 94.8% of the norovirus, respectively. When storing food, keep it in a separate container to prevent cross-contamination. Fruits and vegetables stored in the refrigerator after washing should also be washed again before eating. Food should preferably be heated to at least 85Â°C for 1 minute or longer before eating. Knives and cutting boards should be disinfected, and using separate cooking utensils for vegetables, meat and fish can lower the risk of infection. Wash your hands with soap under running water for at least 30 seconds before handling food. People infected with norovirus should be cautious about dehydration. Drinking boiled water with sugar and salt can help. /AI-generated photo People infected with norovirus develop symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea within 1 to 2 days. Abdominal pain, chills, fever, nausea and muscle aches can also occur. Most people recover naturally after 2 to 3 days, but caution is needed because dehydration can occur. If dehydration is severe, treatment involving intravenous fluid administration may be considered. When symptoms occur, drink plenty of fluids through sports drinks without caffeine or alcohol. The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said it is also helpful to drink boiled water mixed with four tablespoons of sugar and one tablespoon of salt per 1 L. Do not take antidiarrheal or antiemetic medication on your own without a doctor's examination. Once diarrhea symptoms improve, eat small amounts of thin rice porridge or rice gruel. If a family member has norovirus, separate the person's living space from the rest of the household. Disinfect items the patient has touched or used with a mixture of bleach and water in a ratio of 1 to 50. Clothes should preferably be sanitized by washing them at 70Â°C or higher. To be safe, the patient should not prepare food for 3 days after recovering. This article has been translated AI. by Kim Bo Mi View All Articles Copyright Â© Health Chosun. content: Topics Business & Management Carpet Facility Management Hard Floors Health & Safety Infection Control Products Restrooms Technology & Trends Training Follow CMM Facebook X LinkedIn Get Your CMM Magazine Subscription Sign up for the CMM Newsletter Advertise with Us Join ISSA News Magazine Resources Certifications / Standards Safer Choices Product Innovation Showcase Sponsored Content Education Videos Industry Research On-Demand Webinars Follow CMM Facebook X LinkedIn Get Your CMM Magazine Subscription Sign up for the CMM Newsletter Advertise with Us Join ISSA Events ISSA Show Industry Events Upcoming Webinars Follow CMM Facebook X LinkedIn Get Your CMM Magazine Subscription Sign up for the CMM Newsletter Advertise with Us Join ISSA ISSA Media Follow CMM Facebook X LinkedIn Get Your CMM Magazine Subscription Sign up for the CMM Newsletter Advertise with Us Join ISSA Contact Subscribe ADVERTISE Nearly 100 Cases of Norovirus Reported at One Kansas School Norovirus cases are at medium levels nationally October 27, 2026 A Kansas elementary school experienced a norovirus outbreak that affected nearly 100 people, Johnson County Health officials said. The outbreak at Bentwood Elementary School in Olathe, Kansas, began in early October and spread to 95 cases among students and staff and two among family members in the Kansas City metropolitan area. Two of the cases were confirmed through laboratory testing, and the remaining cases were “epidemiologically linked, meaning individuals experienced similar symptoms around the same time and in the same setting,” officials said. Norovirus is the leading cause of vomiting, diarrhea and foodborne illness in the United States, and people of all ages can get infected and sick with norovirus, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. According to school and county health officials, people impacted by the outbreak at Bentwood Elementary experienced symptoms including vomiting, diarrhea, nausea and stomach pain. Officials said no hospitalizations were reported, and no new cases have been reported since Oct. 13. Throughout the outbreak, the local health department has worked closely with school officials to monitor illnesses, provide public health guidance and help prevent further spread. While the outbreak is considered over, local teams will continue to monitor the situation. Annually, around 21 million Americans are diagnosed with norovirus. The virus is incredibly contagious and frequently reported in school settings, where children interact in close quarters. The CDC said the most effective way to prevent norovirus spread is washing hands with soap and water. Hand sanitizer does not kill norovirus. Current CDC data shows that norovirus cases are at medium levels nationally, without significant spikes. Tags U.S. Green Building Council Streamlines Zero Waste Certification October 27, 2026 Last week, the U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC) launched TRUE v2—the next iteration of the TRUE (Total Resource Use and Efficiency) zero waste certification program. The new version of the rating system emphasizes zero waste impacts and global applicability, and it helps organizations advance their decarbonization, business transformation and circularity goals. For more than 10 years, TRUE has reshaped waste operations for organizations, companies and small businesses, with over 680 certified projects totaling 272 million square feet and diverting 8.9 million tons of waste from landfills. The streamlined rating system collects, measures, benchmarks and verifies sustainability performance. Updates to the TRUE v2 rating system include: Rebalanced credit structure to support projects starting their zero-waste journey while also rewarding high performers. Improved global usability with clearer, internationally applicable language and approaches. Greater rewards for higher-impact and harder-to-achieve actions. TRUE v2 comes as more organizations seek clarity on zero waste roadmaps, with waste volumes rising, landfill capacity tightening, and disposal costs escalating. The Global Waste Management Outlook 2024 projects that the direct cost of waste management could double by 2050, and the Environmental Research and Education Foundation found that commercial waste disposal costs in the U.S. have grown by 15-30% since 2016. TRUE v2 was developed with USGBC members and stakeholders, including the TRUE Advisory Council, and informed by global public consultation from zero waste practitioners. Registration for TRUE v2 is now open on the Arc platform for projects interested in advancing their zero waste goals and pursuing certification.
